title: Early arranging and learning from stock arrangements
summary: Carter explains laying out stock arrangement parts on the floor and arranging directly in transposed keys.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Okay, I'd like to ask a few questions about your early arranging and composing. Dickie Wells, in his book, mentions that you arranged for Billy Fowler. Is that correct? Were you arranging that early?
What years or year was that?

Well, I'm not quite sure, because the earliest one that survives on records, as far as I know, is with Charlie Johnson, and that's 1928. And that's "Charleston Is the Best Dance." Now that's on recordings -- but he's not referring to recordings here.

Well, as far as my memory serves me, it seems that I started arranging when I was with Charlie Johnson. Now maybe I had done something earlier with Billy Fowler, which would have been just writing some saxophone choruses, you know, without rhythm parts, you know...
Uh huh.
The things that were already familiar to, you know, bass, piano, drums and guitar. So maybe I did do something at that time, but it would have been limited to that, I believe.

Uh huh. Okay. You mentioned this before -- and maybe this is a little bit redundant, but you mentioned how stock arrangements were taken and then converted in to other arrangements, or how you used the plan of parts from stock arrangements to make your own arrangements
at a very early stage in your arranging career. Can you sort of describe that process?

Oh. Well, all I meant by that was that I didn't know anything about making a score; I hadn't studied orchestrating or instrumentation or composition at that time, and I just used to take the parts of an orchestra, either by Arthur Lang or Walter Paul or Don Redman, or, what are some of the other names? Archie Bleyer, who came a little later.
Jack Mason.

Jack Mason, Jimmy Dale ... people like that who were doing those things at that time -- and I would just take the parts and lay them out on the floor, and you know, first, second trumpet and trombone, and the two tenors and the alto -- I think that's the way it used to be in those days, just three brass, and three rhythm, and I started arranging like that. I would arrange ...
And these were all transposed, then; these were not in ...

Oh, no ... not in concert key. I started arranging immediately in the respective keys, making the lead trumpet part first. Well, of course, this was the hard way -- but I didn't realize that until later. At that stage, anyway, it was the hard way.
Uh huh. Now when you did this,
in what fashion -- I mean, were you adapting some of these, or ...
Oh no. I was just watching the form, how it was done.
You were doing your own arrangements?
I beg your pardon?
When you were doing original things, that is -- you weren't taking these stock arrangements and transforming them.

Oh, not at all. I would make another arrangement on another song that I'd see ... I'd just see how they, you know, did the parts, and you know, how to do everything, that's all. Everything except make a score, that is.
